@graph.name: Miso Eggplant Stir-Fry
@graph.description: You only need one pan and 20 minutes! Cut the eggplant into bite-sized chunks, then sear until tender and stir in a simple miso sauce. Enjoy it as a savory Japanese side dish or over hot rice. It's a keeper in my kitchen!

itemListElement.text: Peel 1 inch ginger and grate using a ceramic grater to yield  ½ tsp grated ginger with juice. Thinly slice 1 green onion/scallion.
itemListElement.name: Peel 1 inch ginger and grate using a ceramic grater to yield  ½ tsp grated ginger with juice. Thinly slice 1 green onion/scallion.

itemListElement.text: In a small bowl, whisk 1 Tbsp miso, 2 Tbsp sake, 2 Tbsp mirin, 1 tsp soy sauce, and ½ tsp grated ginger until smooth.
itemListElement.name: In a small bowl, whisk 1 Tbsp miso, 2 Tbsp sake, 2 Tbsp mirin, 1 tsp soy sauce, and ½ tsp grated ginger until smooth.

itemListElement.text: Cut 3 Japanese eggplants into bite-size pieces using the Japanese rangiri (rotational cut) technique.Nami's Tip: The angled rangiri cut gives each piece more surface area, so it cooks faster and picks up more of the sauce. Eggplant browns quickly once cut, so slice it right before you're ready to cook.

Eggplant browns quickly once cut, so slice it right before you're ready to cook.

itemListElement.text: Heat a large frying pan over medium heat. Add 1 Tbsp neutral oil and 1 Tbsp toasted sesame oil, swirling to coat the surface evenly, then add the eggplant.
itemListElement.name: Heat a large frying pan over medium heat. Add 1 Tbsp neutral oil and 1 Tbsp toasted sesame oil, swirling to coat the surface evenly, then add the eggplant.

itemListElement.text: Sear the eggplant undisturbed for 1½–3 minutes until golden brown. Flip and cook for another 1½–3 minutes until tender.
itemListElement.name: Sear the eggplant undisturbed for 1½–3 minutes until golden brown. Flip and cook for another 1½–3 minutes until tender.

itemListElement.text: Pour in the miso sauce and toss quickly, shaking the pan. Cook for 30–60 seconds until the sauce thickens and clings to the eggplant, then immediately remove from heat.Nami's Tip: Miso burns quickly because of its sugar content, so keep a close eye on the pan and take it off the heat as soon as the sauce thickens.

itemListElement.text: Transfer to a plate, garnish with sliced green onion, and serve warm with hot steamed rice.
itemListElement.name: Transfer to a plate, garnish with sliced green onion, and serve warm with hot steamed rice.

itemListElement.text: Keep the leftovers in an airtight container and store in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Don't freeze it, because eggplant turns watery once thawed.

@graph.name: Can I make this without a wok?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes! A large skillet works well. A carbon steel pan is the best substitute for a wok because it’s much lighter than cast iron, handles high heat, and develops a natural nonstick patina. However, any well-preheated skillet will give the eggplant a great sear.

@graph.name: What type of miso should I use?

acceptedAnswer.text: White miso offers a sweeter, milder flavor from a shorter fermentation. Red miso ferments longer for a deeper, saltier umami kick. If your miso contains added dashi stock, taste your sauce first and slightly reduce the soy sauce.

@graph.name: Can I use a globe eggplant?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. If you cannot find Japanese or Chinese eggplants, globe eggplants are a good substitute (they just have a thicker skin). Keep the skin on and cut the pieces into uniform wedges so they hold their shape without getting mushy.
